Wash
wosh
v.t. (rendering Hebrew rachats/kabas, Greek louō/niptō)
From Saxon wascan. Hebrew distinguishes what English merges: rachats is to wash the body, kabas is to wash clothes by treading or beating them. Greek keeps a similar distinction: louō is to bathe the whole body, niptō to wash a part, and the difference carries real doctrine in John 13.

Biblical Definition

Washing runs through Scripture as the standing figure for cleansing from sin, and the Bible is careful to say who does it. David does not offer to wash himself: “Wash me throughly from mine iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin” (Psalm 51:2). Isaiah's command to wash is immediately explained as repentance and the abandoning of evil doings: “Wash you, make you clean; put away the evil of your doings from before mine eyes; cease to do evil” (Isaiah 1:16). The Lord Jesus, kneeling with a towel, makes the washing of feet the sign of an absolute necessity: “If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me” (John 13:8) — and when Peter overcorrects and asks for his hands and head too, the answer draws the great distinction: he that is bathed needeth only to wash his feet. And Ananias puts it to Saul as a summons that will not wait: “arise, and be baptized, and wash away thy sins, calling on the name of the Lord” (Acts 22:16). Taken together the passages hold the whole doctrine: the bath of regeneration happens once and is God's work; the daily washing of defiled feet is the ongoing confession of a man already clean; and no one washes himself into a standing with God.

Webster 1828 Definition

To cleanse by water or other liquid; to purify. In Scripture, the prayer to be washed throughly from iniquity, the command to wash and put away evil doings, Christ's word that unless He washes a man he has no part with Him, and the summons to be baptized and wash away sins.

expand to see more

WASH, v.t. 1. To cleanse by ablution, or by rubbing in water; to free from dirt or filth by water.

2. To overflow or dash upon; as, waves washing the shore.

3. To purify from guilt or defilement; to cleanse morally.

4. From Saxon wascan; Hebrew rachats, to wash the body, and kabas, to wash garments.

5. In Scripture, wash me throughly from mine iniquity, Ps. 51; if I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me, John 13.

Key Scripture

Psalm 51:2 — "Wash me throughly from mine iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin."

Isaiah 1:16 — "Wash you, make you clean; put away the evil of your doings from before mine eyes; cease to do evil;"

John 13:8 — "Peter saith unto him, Thou shalt never wash my feet. Jesus answered him, If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me."

Acts 22:16 — "And now why tarriest thou? arise, and be baptized, and wash away thy sins, calling on the name of the Lord."

Modern Corruption

Baptismal washing is made the instrument that itself removes sin, so that the sign is confused with the thing signified; and, in reaction, the daily washing of a believer's defilement is neglected as though confession were unnecessary once a man is justified.

expand to see more

Acts 22:16 is the standing proof text for baptismal regeneration, and the reading has to ignore the rest of Scripture to stand. Cornelius received the Holy Ghost before he was baptized; the thief on the cross went to paradise unbaptized; Abraham was justified by faith and received circumcision afterward as a seal of the righteousness he already had. Baptism is a sign and seal of the washing away of sins, and Scripture regularly speaks of the sign in the language of the thing signified, exactly as it says the cup is the new testament in His blood. What washes is the blood of Christ applied by the Spirit — unto him that loved us, and washed us from our sins in his own blood. The water preaches that, seals it to the believer, and never replaces it. Where the sign is made the instrument, men are sent to the font instead of to Christ.

The opposite neglect is the more common failure among the sound. John 13 distinguishes the bath from the foot-washing: the disciple who is bathed is clean every whit and does not need bathing again, but his feet get dirty walking, and they must be washed. That is the doctrine of daily confession in a picture. Justification is once for all and cannot be repeated; fellowship is disturbed by sin and is restored by confession, since if we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us. A believer who ignores his feet on the ground that he is already bathed will find his communion cold and his conscience dull, and he will have no explanation for it. The principle to recover keeps both: one bath, many washings, and Christ Himself kneeling with the basin.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew rachats, to wash the body; kabas, to wash garments by treading; Greek louō, to bathe wholly, niptō, to wash a part, and apolouō, to wash away.

expand to see more

Hebrew rachats (H7364) — to wash or bathe the body; the priests washed at the laver before serving (Exodus 30:19-21).

Hebrew kabas (H3526) — to wash clothes by treading or beating; used in Psalm 51:2, “wash me throughly.”

Greek louō (G3068) — to bathe the whole body; “he that is washed needeth not save to wash his feet” (John 13:10).

Greek niptō (G3538) — to wash a part of the body; the foot-washing of John 13.

Greek apolouō (G628) — to wash away, wash off; “wash away thy sins” (Acts 22:16) and “ye are washed” (1 Corinthians 6:11).

Usage

"Of cleansing sought from God alone: Wash me throughly from mine iniquity (Psalm 51:2)."

"Of the necessity of Christ's cleansing: If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me (John 13:8)."

"Of the summons to the new convert: arise, and be baptized, and wash away thy sins (Acts 22:16)."
